why: Two textbook linked-list moves glued together: reverse the first k nodes in place (Reverse Linked List II on a prefix), then split into two stable chains with dummy-tail pointers (Odd Even / Partition List) and weave them alternately like Merge Two Lists with a turn flag.
hints: Break it into three passes: reverse a prefix, split into two chains, weave the chains.

Reversing the first k nodes: the usual prev/cur/next loop k times, then reconnect the old head (now the k-th node) to the rest. Splitting: walk once and append each node to the 'divisible' or 'other' chain, which keeps each chain's order.
Weave by alternating chains, starting with divisible; when one chain runs out, append the rest of the other. Each node is relinked a constant number of times: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
pitfalls: k = 0 means no reversal; k = n reverses the whole list.
Zero and negative multiples are divisible; Python's % with a positive divisor already gives 0 for them.
Cut each node's next pointer as you move it into a chain, or the old links create a cycle.
